strengths: Novel core idea (module switching instead of weight averaging) for post-training backdoor defense, motivated by a clean intuition that backdoor shortcuts are localized and asymmetrically placed across compromised models.

Solid theoretical grounding on two-layer linear/non-linear networks (Theorem 1, Proposition 1) showing module-switched models achieve higher backdoor divergence than weight-averaged models, with empirical validation of the second-order term omission and utility-preservation identities in the appendix.

Very broad and thorough empirical evaluation spanning text (SST-2, MNLI, AG News with RoBERTa/BERT/DeBERTa) and vision (CIFAR-10, TinyImageNet with ViT/ResNet-18/50), multiple attack types (insertion, syntactic, warping, patch-based, adaptive), varying poison rates, three- and four-model fusion, collusive-backdoor and label-inconsistent settings.

Practical design choices: requires only 2 models (vs. 3-6 for prior merging defenses), needs only 20-50 clean samples per class and no poisoned data, and the searched switching strategy is reusable/transferable across same-architecture models, giving a favorable amortized efficiency profile (Table 3).
Reasonably comprehensive ablations (heuristic rule removal, early-stopping vs full search, structural-overlap/diversity analysis, candidate-selection quality) that support the design choices.

Good coverage of adaptive/adversarial scenarios (attacker aware of the switching strategy, Adaptive-Patch attack, identical/colluding backdoors) that are often missing in related model-merging defense papers.
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis is restricted to two-layer (effectively linear) networks; the extension to deep Transformers/CNNs in Section 4 relies purely on heuristic rules with no formal argument that the same divergence guarantees hold, leaving a meaningful theory-practice gap for the main claimed contribution.

Empirical results are inconsistent in places: e.g., on MNLI (Table 8) MSD is worse than WAG for BadNet+LWS (57.0 vs 64.3, better) but for LWS+Hidden MSD (63.8) is essentially tied or worse than WAG (62.7); similarly in the candidate-selection analysis (Table 15) the selected candidate is sometimes outperformed by an unselected one, undermining the strength of the 'guaranteed improvement' narrative.

The five heuristic scoring rules (Section 4.2/H.1) and their weighting (all λ=1.0) appear largely hand-designed without principled justification or sensitivity analysis beyond simple ablation of three of the five terms; no analysis of how these choices scale to much larger/deeper architectures (e.g., LLM-scale models) is provided.

Baseline comparison omits some directly relevant recent merging-based defenses explicitly discussed in related work (e.g., DAM, Yang et al. 2025), which is presented as a close competitor requiring more models but is never empirically compared.

The threat/defender model assumes access to "as few as two" domain-relevant models of uncertain integrity from the same architecture family, which, while more practical than prior work, is still a non-trivial assumption that may not hold in many real single-model deployment scenarios.

Scope is limited to classification tasks (explicitly acknowledged as a limitation); no evidence on generative or instruction-tuned LLMs, which are increasingly the dominant post-training deployment scenario motivating the paper's introduction.
The evolutionary search, while offline, still takes hours (2.6-4.3h) and its scalability to models with far more modules/layers (e.g., 70B+ parameter LLMs) or heterogeneous architectures is untested.

strengths: The paper offers a theoretical analysis (Theorem 1, Proposition 1) for two-layer linear networks that formally shows module-switched models have higher average and worst-case backdoor divergence than weight-averaged (WAG) models, and derives a matching utility-preservation identity, giving the method at least a partial theoretical grounding not offered by prior model-merging defenses.

The empirical evaluation is broad in scope, spanning NLP (SST-2, MNLI, AG News) and vision (CIFAR-10, TinyImageNet) datasets, multiple backdoor attacks (BadNet, InsertSent, LWS, HiddenKiller, WaNet, BATT, PhysicalBA, Adaptive-Patch), and multiple architectures (RoBERTa, BERT, DeBERTa, ViT, ResNet-18/50), with numerous ablations (heuristic rules, clean-data budget, poisoning rate, collusive/label-inconsistent backdoors, adaptive attacker).

The proposed defense addresses a practically relevant limitation of prior merging-based defenses (needing 3-6 homologous models) by working with as few as two models, and the strategy-reuse/transferability property (search once, reuse across architectures) is a useful practical advantage supported by an efficiency comparison against DARE/TIES/WAG.

The paper considers an interesting and underexplored threat scenario of collusive backdoors shared across models, where WAG degenerates but MSD remains more resilient, which is a reasonable and somewhat novel contribution to the model-merging defense literature.
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis (Section 3) is restricted to two-layer, largely linear networks, and its extension to deep Transformer/CNN architectures (Section 4) is purely heuristic (ad hoc adjacency/balance/diversity scoring in the fitness function) with no formal argument connecting the fitness score to actual backdoor suppression in nonlinear, multi-layer models; the claimed link between fitness score and empirical defense (Section 5.2, Table 14) is based on a single anecdotal comparison rather than a systematic correlation study.

The heuristic-rule ablation in Table 16 partially contradicts the paper's own narrative: for the BadNet+Hidden setting, removing rule 1 actually *improves* average ASR (23.4 vs. 34.1 for the full rule set), which undercuts the claim that "removing any rule typically degrades performance" and is not adequately discussed or explained.

Reported gains over WAG/DARE/TIES are inconsistent at the level of individual attacks even when the averaged ASR is lower (e.g., in Table 8's BadNet+InsertSent combination, DARE achieves a much lower ASR on BadNet (11.6 vs. 24.8) even though MSD wins on average); such cherry-picked averaging across a large number of tables raises concern about selective emphasis on favorable comparisons.

The defender capability assumptions (white-box access to at least two domain-relevant, potentially trojaned models, plus a small labeled clean validation set) remain a meaningful practical constraint that is not clearly weaker than what several baselines require, somewhat undercutting the motivating narrative about post-training defenses with minimal resources.

The search algorithm's cost (2.6–4.3 hours per architecture) and the need to rerun search with different seeds to defend against adaptive attackers (Section J.11) suggest the "one-time offline" framing understates the operational overhead in adversarial settings where the strategy may need periodic refreshing.

CNN experiments (ResNet-18/50) are comparatively thin, covering only two attack combinations each versus much more extensive Transformer/ViT evaluation, limiting confidence in the claimed cross-architecture generality.

Candidate-selection results (Table 15) show that the selection heuristic sometimes fails to pick the best candidate (unselected candidates occasionally achieve lower ASR), and no principled guarantee or deeper analysis is given for why the feature-distance heuristic reliably approximates the theoretically motivated "most divergent" candidate in deep, nonlinear models.

strengths: Well-motivated, practically relevant problem: post-training backdoor defense without training data or trusted references
Novel and intuitive core idea (module switching vs. weight averaging) grounded in a clean theoretical toy-model analysis (Theorem 1, Proposition 1) with full proofs
Thorough empirical validation of underlying assumptions (e.g., negligibility of second-order interaction terms) and utility-preservation identity

Broad experimental coverage across multiple architectures (RoBERTa, BERT, DeBERTa, ViT, ResNet-18/50), attacks (BadNet, InsertSent, LWS, HiddenKiller, WaNet, BATT, PhysicalBA, Adaptive-Patch), poison rates, and challenging scenarios (collusive backdoors, label-inconsistent attacks, adaptive attackers)
Practical efficiency: one-time offline architecture-dependent search reused across models, fast candidate selection with minimal clean data (20-50 samples/class)
Extensive ablations supporting design choices (heuristic rule contributions, early stopping vs. full search, strategy diversity/overlap, candidate selection quality)
Clear algorithmic presentation and stated commitment to code release supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Theoretical results rely on strong simplifications (two-layer, mostly linear networks, iid Gaussian synthetic perturbations) and the extension to deep, nonlinear Transformer/CNN architectures via heuristic rules is more intuitive than rigorously justified
Heuristic scoring rules and their equal weighting (all lambda_k=1.0), as well as the specific residual-decay factor, appear somewhat ad hoc without deeper sensitivity analysis
Missing comparison to closely related and directly cited selective module-substitution work (e.g., Tong et al. 2024) which seems like a natural and important baseline

Some experimental results are mixed or only marginal improvements over WAG (e.g., certain ResNet BadNet+WaNet cases, some SST-2 combinations where MSD ranks second), slightly undercutting claims of consistent superiority

No ablation isolating the contribution of the evolutionary search itself versus simply using the heuristic scoring function directly or random strategies, given the search relies on non-differentiable proxy objectives rather than actual backdoor mitigation feedback
Scope explicitly limited to classification tasks and data-poisoning attacks; generative model backdoors are unaddressed
Threat model assumption of having multiple domain-relevant, architecture-matched models of uncertain integrity may be less commonly satisfied in practice than single-model defense scenarios
